character_and_relationship_context: Ingrid Lindgren is a woman in her mid-thirties with a pragmatic, slightly stern expression that softens only when she speaks to her mother. She dresses in well-cut, understated clothes—wool blazers, comfortable trousers, leather brogues—practical for overseeing housekeeping and meeting contractors, but the quality reveals inherited taste. Each morning she reviews occupancy reports and breakfast costs on her tablet while her mother eats oatmeal, answering each repeated question with the same even tone, never correcting or sighing, but when her mother turns away she makes a quick note on her phone—a reminder to reorder hand soap or call the plumber. Her mother has early-stage dementia; Ingrid has reconfigured the hotel’s ground-floor linen closet into a small bedroom with a courtyard view so her mother can wander safely while Ingrid works at the front desk. The night nurse arrives at 9 p.m., allowing Ingrid to attend regional business conferences where she sits in the front row, asking pointed questions about average revenue per available room and tax incentives. She is known for short, precise emails and her habit of standing with arms crossed while listening, then leaning forward when making a counteroffer. She inherited a fortune from her grandparents—her grandfather owned a chain of hardware stores in the 1970s—but she is eager to prove she can build something of her own. The hotel in Gamla Stan was a deliberate choice; she stayed there once as a child with her mother, and the memory of cobblestones and oak doors felt like a claim on her past. She keeps a spreadsheet of every guest complaint and compliment, and has trained staff to offer a free glass of glögg to any returning visitor. Her competitiveness surfaces most clearly when she discusses expansion: she wants a second property within two years, preferably a smaller boutique hotel in Södermalm for a younger crowd. She has walked the property three times and prepared a detailed comparison of renovation costs versus projected yield. In negotiations with contractors she never shows hesitation, even when secretly calculating whether the margin will hold. The tension between her ambition and devotion to her mother is visible in small ways: she never schedules meetings after 8 p.m., and keeps a framed photo of her mother on the office desk next to a stack of loan applications. She grew up in a town outside Uppsala, where her father was a high school teacher and her mother a librarian; the inheritance came as a surprise. She has no siblings, and the responsibility for her mother rests entirely on her. On Sundays she closes the hotel for two hours and takes her mother for a walk along the waterfront, talking softly about the ships and gulls, never mentioning the business. It is the only time she allows herself to stop planning. Karin was Ingrid's closest friend in secondary school; they now meet only during Karin's infrequent visits to Stockholm. Ingrid often continues working during free evenings, but she once canceled a contractor meeting to see Karin. She usually prioritizes her mother's schedule over last-minute plans.
objective_situation: Ingrid's phone buzzes with a text from Karin, a friend from her Uppsala childhood who now lives abroad. Karin is in Stockholm for the day and suggests meeting for fika at a café near Gamla Stan. Ingrid has no pressing meetings, and her mother is calmly reading in the courtyard. The night nurse will arrive at 9 p.m., so she has a few hours free. She considers whether to accept the invitation or politely decline to continue reviewing her hotel expansion estimates.
state_and_available_memories: Ingrid's shoulders are tight from hours hunched over financial estimates. Her mother is quietly reading in the courtyard. She has no pressing meetings, but the expansion estimates still need another pass. Immediate memories: Karin's name on the phone brings back skipping class together by the river in Uppsala. The café reminds her of the almond pastry they shared on Karin's last visit. Reflective memories: Ingrid remembers that Karin never asked about her inheritance, and their conversations felt separate from her hotel life. She also recalls her mother telling her that youth friendships are worth preserving.
name: Ingrid Lindgren
scenario_title: Fika Invitation from an Old Friend
